lines.text: Bronze kings, emperors and revolutionaries, inventions that changed the world, and a rise that changed it again. This is the story of China, over more than three thousand years.
Along the Yellow River, the Shang kings ruled a Bronze Age realm. Their royal tombs at Anyang held fine bronze vessels and the earliest Chinese writing.
That writing was scratched on oracle bones to question the spirits. The same characters, much changed, are still written across China today.
The Zhou overthrew the Shang and claimed the Mandate of Heaven, the idea that rulers govern only while heaven approves. Their rule lasted for centuries.
Rival states began raising walls along the northern frontier, the first pieces of what would become the Great Wall.
In these restless times, tradition places the general Sun Tzu, credited with The Art of War, though little about his life is certain.
Work began on the Grand Canal, which over many centuries would grow into the longest waterway ever dug, carrying grain between north and south.
As Zhou power faded, seven great states fought for supremacy. For two and a half centuries, the Warring States tore at one another.
The state of Qin won. Its king conquered the rest and took a new title, First Emperor. He made one writing, one coinage and one set of measures.
In 221 before the common era, China was united as an empire for the first time, to be ruled by dynasties for over two thousand years.
The Qin dynasty itself was brief and harsh. It linked the frontier walls and laid the foundations every later empire built on.
When the First Emperor died, thousands of life-size clay soldiers were buried to guard him. Farmers found them by chance in 1974, each with its own face.
The Han dynasty followed and lasted four centuries. It trained officials in Confucian learning, and most Chinese people still call themselves Han.
Under the Han, the historian Sima Qian wrote the Records of the Grand Historian, the model for official histories ever after.
Han China also gave the world paper, made from pressed plant fibres. It would travel west and transform learning everywhere.
Han envoys opened routes into Central Asia, and the Silk Road began to carry silk, spices, ideas and faiths across a continent.
As the Han crumbled, allied armies defeated the warlord Cao Cao on the Yangtze at Red Cliffs, a battle retold for centuries.
The empire split into three rival kingdoms, Wei, Shu and Wu. Their generals and schemes became some of China's best loved stories.
After nearly three hundred years of division, the Sui reunited north and south, and dug the Grand Canal on a vast scale. Their costly wars soon brought them down.
The Tang took their place and ruled a golden age, with a great capital at Chang'an, busy trade along the Silk Road and a flowering of poetry.
Under the Tang rose Wu Zetian, who began as a concubine and became the only woman ever to rule China as emperor in her own name.
This was the age of Li Bai, poet of wine, moonlight and wandering. Children in China still learn his short poems by heart.
His friend Du Fu wrote of war, hunger and the suffering of ordinary people. Together they are remembered as the two great poets of their age.
Then the general An Lushan rose against the throne. The rebellion cost millions of lives, and the Tang never fully recovered.
Chinese alchemists searching for an elixir of life found something else, gunpowder. It brought fireworks, and in time it changed warfare across the world.
The Song dynasty became an age of commerce and invention, its cities among the largest on Earth.
Song sailors were steering by the magnetic compass, a needle that had first been used for fortune telling.
And around the same time, Bi Sheng printed with movable clay type, centuries before Gutenberg in Europe.
From the north came the Mongols. Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis, completed the conquest of the Song.
He ruled all China as the Yuan dynasty from Khanbaliq, today's Beijing, and welcomed foreign traders to his court.
Writers looked back to the old wars. Romance of the Three Kingdoms turned that era into a great historical novel.
In 1368 the Ming drove out the Mongols. They would build much of the Great Wall as it stands today.
Ming fleets under Admiral Zheng He sailed seven times across the Indian Ocean, as far as Arabia and East Africa.
In Beijing the Ming built the Forbidden City, the palace of emperors for almost five hundred years.
Journey to the West, with its mischievous Monkey King, became another of China's great classical novels.
In the north, the Manchus founded the Qing. They took Beijing and expanded the empire to its greatest size.
The Kangxi Emperor reigned for sixty-one years, crushing a southern rebellion, taking Taiwan and sponsoring a great dictionary.
In Qing times came Dream of the Red Chamber, the tale of a noble family's rise and fall, often called the finest Chinese novel.
In the troubled nineteenth century, the Empress Dowager Cixi ruled from behind the throne for decades as regent for two child emperors.
When China banned the opium trade, Britain went to war. China lost, gave up Hong Kong and opened its ports.
Then came the Taiping Rebellion, led by a man who called himself the younger brother of Jesus. It was one of the deadliest wars in history.
A young doctor, Sun Yat-sen, began plotting revolution against the weakened Qing.
The writer Lu Xun would attack old habits in sharp stories written in everyday speech, founding modern Chinese literature.
Chiang Kai-shek would rise to lead the Nationalists and fight the long war against Japan.
Mao Zedong, born to a farming family in Hunan, would lead the Communists to victory and reshape the country.
Beside him stood Zhou Enlai, who would serve as premier for more than a quarter of a century.
At the turn of the century, the Boxers rose against foreign influence and besieged the legations in Beijing, until eight foreign powers marched in.
Deng Xiaoping, born in Sichuan, would one day open China to the world.
And Puyi became emperor at the age of two, the last ever to sit on the dragon throne.
In 1911 revolution swept the Qing away, ending two thousand years of imperial rule.
The Republic of China was born, with Sun Yat-sen as its first president, but it was soon torn apart by warlords.
In Shanghai in 1921, a small group founded the Chinese Communist Party.
Before long, Nationalists and Communists were at war, a struggle that would last more than twenty years.
Surrounded, the Red Army broke out and marched thousands of kilometres across rough country. On the Long March, Mao took the lead.
In 1937 Japan invaded. Millions of Chinese people died before Japan surrendered in 1945.
Mao proclaimed the People's Republic in 1949. Within a year, Chinese troops were fighting American-led forces in Korea.
In 1953, Xi Jinping was born, the son of a revolutionary veteran and a future leader of the party.
Mao's Great Leap Forward drove people into communes and backyard steel furnaces, and farming was thrown into chaos.
Famine followed, one of the deadliest in history. Many millions starved, and the full toll is still debated.
A boy born in Hangzhou in 1964, Jack Ma, would grow up to build Alibaba, one of the world's largest online marketplaces.
Mao then launched the Cultural Revolution. Red Guards attacked teachers and officials, schools shut, and millions were persecuted over ten years.
After Mao's death, Deng Xiaoping turned China around, letting farmers and firms sell for profit and inviting foreign investment. Decades of rapid growth began.
At the same time, most couples were limited to one child, a rule enforced harshly for more than thirty years.
In 1989 students filled Tiananmen Square calling for reform. In early June the army cleared the square.
In 1997 Hong Kong returned from British to Chinese rule, under the promise of one country, two systems.
On the Yangtze rose the Three Gorges Dam, the world's largest hydroelectric station, which displaced more than a million people.
That autumn, Yang Liwei orbited the Earth for about a day, and China became the third nation to send a person into space.
In 2008 a powerful earthquake struck Sichuan, bringing down buildings, schools among them, and prompting a vast relief effort.
That summer Beijing hosted the Olympic Games, opening with a spectacular ceremony in the new Bird's Nest stadium.
Two years later, Shanghai's World Expo drew one of the biggest crowds such a fair has ever seen.
Under Xi Jinping, China announced the Belt and Road, funding ports, railways and roads across three continents.
China's Chang'e 4 became the first spacecraft ever to land on the far side of the Moon.
In Hong Kong, months of mass protests for democracy ended when Beijing imposed a national security law.
Meanwhile a new coronavirus, first found in China, spread around the world, bringing lockdowns and years of disruption.
In 2021 China began building its own space station, Tiangong, where its astronauts now live for months at a time.
And in 2022 Beijing hosted the Winter Games, the first city to host both the Summer and Winter Olympics.
From oracle bones to the far side of the Moon, China's long story is still being written.
